entry: Innermost geologic layer of [[Earth]], a solid ball of iron–nickel alloy. It has a radius of about 1,230 km (760 mi), roughly 20% of Earth's radius and 70% of the [[Moon|Moon's]] radius. Its surface temperature is estimated at about 5,700 K (5,430 °C; 9,800 °F), similar to the surface of the [[Sun]], and it remains solid because of the high pressure at its depth. Lighter elements such as [[Oxygen|oxygen]] and [[Sulfur|sulfur]] are thought to be present along with iron and nickel. The inner core was deduced in 1936 by the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann from seismograms of earthquakes in New Zealand. Its rigidity was confirmed in 1971, and in 2005 shear waves were detected passing through it. It grows by about 1 millimeter per year as material from the outer core solidifies at its boundary, and its interaction with the convecting outer core helps sustain the geodynamo that generates [[Earth's magnetic field]].

Magnetic field extending from [[Earth|Earth's]] interior into space, also called the geomagnetic field. It is generated by electric currents in the convecting molten iron and nickel of the [[Earth's outer core|outer core]], a process called a geodynamo. In a 2019 survey its strength at the surface ranged around 30,000 to 60,000 nT (0.30 to 0.60 G). The field approximates a magnetic dipole tilted about 11° from Earth's rotational axis. The magnetic poles usually lie near the geographic poles and drift slowly, but at irregular intervals averaging several hundred thousand years the field reverses. Reversals are recorded in igneous rocks as stripes on [[Mid-ocean ridge|mid-ocean ridges]], which helps paleomagnetists track the motion of continents. The magnetosphere deflects most of the solar wind, which would otherwise strip away the ozone layer, and traps charged particles in the [[Van Allen radiation belt|Van Allen radiation belts]]. Humans have used [[Compass|compasses]] for direction-finding since the 11th century.

Layer of silicate rock between Earth's [[Crust (geology)|crust]] and outer core. It makes up about 67% of Earth's mass and 84% of its volume, and it is about 2,900 km (1,800 mi) thick. Predominantly solid, it behaves on geologic time scales as a viscous fluid, sometimes compared to caramel. The mantle is divided into the upper mantle, a transition zone at depths of about 410 to 660 km, and the lower mantle. The upper mantle is composed mainly of peridotite. Partial melting at [[Mid-ocean ridge|mid-ocean ridges]] produces oceanic crust, and partial melting at subduction zones produces continental crust. Convection within the mantle drives [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]] and volcanism.

Path of [[Earth]] around the [[Sun]], an ellipse with the Earth–Sun barycenter as one focus and an eccentricity of 0.0167. At an average distance of 149.60 million km (92.96 million mi), or one [[Astronomical unit|astronomical unit]], Earth completes one orbit in 365.256 days. Its average orbital speed is 29.78 km/s (18.50 mi/s). Combined with the planet's [[Axial tilt|axial tilt]], the orbit produces the seasons.

Fluid layer of mostly [[Iron|iron]] and [[Nickel|nickel]], about 2,260 km (1,400 mi) thick, lying between Earth's inner core and mantle. It begins about 2,889 km (1,795 mi) beneath the surface and ends at 5,150 km (3,200 mi) at the inner core boundary. The core remains liquid because there is not enough pressure to solidify it. Its density is 5 to 10 percent lower than that of iron at Earth's core temperatures and pressures, so lighter elements such as [[Sulfur|sulfur]] and [[Oxygen|oxygen]] are thought to be present. As of 2023, estimates put sulfur at 1.7 percent and oxygen at 0.8 to 5.3 percent of the outer core by weight. Convection in the fluid generates [[Earth's magnetic field]] through a geodynamo.

Spin of [[Earth]] around its axis. Earth turns once in about 24 hours relative to the [[Sun]], and once in 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4 seconds relative to distant stars. Tidal effects of the [[Moon|Moon]] have slowed the rotation, so the day has lengthened by about 2.3 milliseconds per century since the 8th century BCE. Scientists reported in 2020 that Earth had begun to rotate faster. At the equator the rotational speed is about 1,674.7 km/h (1,040.6 mph), decreasing with latitude to zero at the poles.

Soil-dwelling [[Annelid|annelid]] invertebrate, the largest members of the class Oligochaeta. Earthworms live in moist, compost-rich soil and feed on detritus, protozoa, nematodes, [[Bacteria|bacteria]], fungi and [[Algae|algae]], making them among the most important detritivores in nature. Adults range from 10 mm to 3 m in length depending on species. The body is a segmented tube within a tube, usually with setae on all segments, and it lacks a true skeleton, relying instead on fluid-filled coelom chambers that act as a hydrostatic skeleton. Earthworms breathe through the skin. Most are hermaphrodites that exchange sperm when mating, but many species, particularly in the family Lumbricidae, reproduce by parthenogenesis. Their excreta also serve as food, and their burrowing and castings help maintain soil fertility.

Order of [[Insect|insects]] with about 2,000 species in 12 families. The name Dermaptera comes from Greek words for skin and wing, referring to the membranous hindwings folded beneath short forewings. Earwigs have forceps-like pincers called cerci at the rear of the abdomen, used for capturing prey and for defense. They are mostly nocturnal, hiding in small, moist crevices by day, and feed on insects and plants. Earwigs are found on all continents except Antarctica. Many species show maternal care, with females guarding eggs and watching over nymphs until their second molt. The common earwig, *Forficula auricularia*, was introduced into North America from Europe in 1907.

British television [[Soap opera|soap opera]], broadcast on [[BBC|BBC One]] since February 1985. Created by Julia Smith and Tony Holland, it is set in the fictional borough of Walford in the East End of [[London]]. Within eight months of its launch it reached the number one spot in BARB's television ratings, and it has remained among the top-rated series in Britain. More than 30 million people watched its 1986 Christmas Day episode. The program has dealt with controversial subjects, and its 2010 baby swap storyline drew more than 6,000 complaints.

Subregion at the eastern edge of the [[Africa|African]] continent, defined in varying scopes. The United Nations recognizes 18 sovereign states and four territories in the region. It includes the [[Horn of Africa]] to the north, the [[African Great Lakes]] to the west and the Indian Ocean coast to the east. Its climate is mostly arid or semi-arid, and drought and flood cycles have caused food insecurity. The region holds some of the earliest evidence of human ancestors, found in highland areas such as the Rift Valley. Its populations were shaped by the [[Bantu expansion]], a migration of Bantu peoples between 2,500 and 3,000 years ago. Portuguese, English and German colonies were established after European exploration. A 2017 estimate put the population at over 537.9 million.

Marginal sea of the western [[Pacific Ocean]], lying offshore from East China. It is bounded by Kyushu and the Ryukyu Islands of Japan to the east and by Taiwan to the south. It connects with the Sea of Japan through the [[Korea Strait]], with the South China Sea via the [[Taiwan Strait]], and with the Philippine Sea between the Ryukyu Islands. Most of the sea is shallow, with almost three-fourths less than 200 meters (660 ft) deep, and its maximum depth of 2,716 meters (8,911 ft) lies in the Okinawa Trough. The [[Yangtze|Yangtze River]] is the largest river flowing into it. The Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands are administered by Japan but claimed by China and Taiwan, and China and South Korea dispute an exclusive economic zone around Socotra Rock.

Vast interior [[Plain|plain]] extending east of the North European Plain, also called the Russian Plain. Stretching eastward from about 25 degrees of longitude, it comprises several plateaus, including the Central Russian Upland and the Volga Upland. It covers most of the [[Baltic states]], European Russia, [[Belarus]] and [[Ukraine]]. The plain spans approximately 4,000,000 sq km and averages about 170 m (560 ft) in elevation. Its highest point, 480 m (1,574.8 ft), lies in the Bugulma-Belebey Upland near the [[Ural Mountains]]. Major river basins include those of the [[Dnieper]] and the [[Volga]]. It is the greatest mountain-free part of the European landscape.

Former communist state in Central Europe, officially the German Democratic Republic (GDR). Formed on October 7, 1949, in the Soviet occupation zone, it was ruled by the Socialist Unity Party of Germany and is often described as a Soviet satellite state. Its centrally planned economy became the most successful in the [[Eastern Bloc]], but emigration to the West weakened the state, and in 1961 it built the [[Berlin Wall]]. Peaceful protests in [[Leipzig]] and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 led to free elections and, on October 3, 1990, reunification with West Germany.

English and later British joint-stock trading company, founded in 1600 and dissolved in 1874. Formed for trade in the East Indies, it gained control of large parts of the [[India|Indian subcontinent]] and at its peak was the largest corporation in the world by various measures. It accounted for about half of world trade in the mid-1700s and early 1800s, dealing in cotton, silk, indigo, tea, salt and later opium. After the Battle of Plassey in 1757 its territorial rule expanded, and by 1858 it ruled or controlled through treaties most of modern India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. After the Indian Rebellion of 1857 the Government of India Act 1858 transferred control to the Crown, creating the [[British Raj]]. The company mishandled the [[Great Bengal famine of 1770]], in which an estimated 10 million people starved.

Break of communion between the [[Catholic Church]] and the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]], also called the Great Schism. Long-standing differences between the Greek East and Latin West included the *Filioque* clause of the Nicene Creed, the use of leavened or unleavened bread in the [[Eucharist]], iconoclasm, the coronation of [[Charlemagne]] as emperor in 800, and the papal claim to universal jurisdiction. The formal split is conventionally dated to 1054, when Cardinal Humbert excommunicated Patriarch Michael I Cerularius of [[Constantinople]], who excommunicated the legates in turn. Scholars have proposed other dates, including 1009, 1204, 1277 and 1484. The sack of Constantinople during the Fourth Crusade in 1204 deepened the divide. In 1965 Pope Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I nullified the anathemas of 1054, a gesture that did not amount to reunion.

1952 [[Novel|novel]] by [[John Steinbeck]], which he considered his *magnum opus*. Set largely in California's Salinas Valley, it follows the interwoven lives of the Trask and Hamilton families. Steinbeck originally addressed the work to his young sons. Its Trask story reworks the biblical [[Cain and Abel]] story, with themes of free will and the struggle between good and evil. The Hamilton family is said to be based on the family of Steinbeck's maternal grandfather, Samuel Hamilton.

Island and special territory of [[Chile]] in the southeastern [[Pacific Ocean]], known to its inhabitants as Rapa Nui. It is renowned for nearly 1,000 monumental statues called [[Moai|moai]], carved by early Rapa Nui people. Many researchers date Polynesian arrival to about 800, though a 2007 study suggests about 1200. The population, estimated at 2,000 to 3,000 when Europeans arrived in 1722, fell to 111 native inhabitants by 1877 as a result of disease, Peruvian slave raids and emigration. Chile annexed the island in 1888, and in 2007 it gained the constitutional status of a special territory. UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site in 1995. Spanish is its only official language in [[Polynesia]].

Armed insurrection against British rule in Ireland during Easter Week, 1916. Launched by Irish republicans on April 24, it sought an independent Irish Republic while Britain fought [[World War I]]. Rebels seized strategic buildings in [[Dublin]] and proclaimed the republic, but after six days of fighting they surrendered. Sixteen leaders were executed from May 1916, and the executions helped build support for independence. Of the 485 people killed, 260 were civilians. The 1918 general election, in which Sinn Féin won 73 of 105 Irish seats, reflected the shift in opinion.

Christian celebration and cultural holiday commemorating the [[Resurrection]] of [[Jesus]]. Described in the New Testament as occurring on the third day after his crucifixion, it culminates the Passion of Jesus and follows Lent, a 40-day period of [[Fasting|fasting]] and penance. The First Council of Nicaea (325) set its date as the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the [[Equinox|vernal equinox]], calculated on a lunisolar basis like the [[Hebrew calendar]]. The English name may derive from the Anglo-Saxon goddess Ēostre, and in most European languages the holiday shares its name with the Jewish [[Passover]]. Customs include sunrise services, the decoration and breaking of eggs, the Easter lily and the Easter Bunny.

Historical region of the eastern [[Arabian Peninsula]], stretching along the Persian Gulf coast from Basra to Khasab. Known as the Bahrain Region, its coastal strip was called Bahrain for a millennium. It now includes parts of Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Its peoples shared a seafaring culture and, historically, moved and married across the area without regard to modern borders. The Bronze Age trading center of Dilmun, in present-day Bahrain, supplied copper, ivory, pearls and dates to Mesopotamian ports. Archaeological evidence shows settlements and burial complexes indicating prosperity from prehistoric times through the Sasanian era. Oil discoveries in the modern era transformed the region's economies.

Unofficial coalition of communist states aligned with the [[Soviet Union]] during the Cold War, from 1947 to 1991. Its members followed Marxism–Leninism and opposed the capitalist Western Bloc, and the bloc was often called the Second World. In Europe it generally comprised the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact countries: East Germany, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and Albania. Elsewhere it included Mongolia, North Vietnam, Laos, North Korea, China and, from 1961, Cuba. Non-Marxist socialist governments, such as those of Iraq, Libya and Yemen, are sometimes considered part of the bloc. The bloc dissolved amid the revolutions of 1989 and the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.

23 Eastern Christian autonomous (*sui iuris*) particular churches in full communion with the pope in Rome. Their roughly 18 million members are a small minority of the Catholic Church's 1.3 billion, concentrated in Eastern Europe, Eastern Africa, the Middle East and India. As of 2022 the largest is the Syro-Malabar Church, followed by the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church. With the exception of the Maronite Church, most were formerly part of Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox or Church of the East communions. Each keeps its own liturgical traditions and canon law, and many allow married men to be ordained as priests, though not as bishops.

Family of Christian church traditions originating in the Eastern Mediterranean region during classical and late antiquity. The term does not refer to a single communion and is contrasted with Western Christianity, centered on the Latin Church. The [[Eastern Orthodox Church]] is the largest body, with a worldwide population of 220 million, followed by the Oriental Orthodox Churches at 60 million. The [[Eastern Catholic Churches]] number about 16–18 million, and the Assyrian Church of the East and Ancient Church of the East have about 400,000 members. The distinction grew out of the division of the Roman Empire in 395 and the cultural divide between the Hellenistic East and the Latin West.

Subregion of the European continent, a largely ambiguous term with geopolitical, cultural and socio-economic connotations. Its eastern boundary is conventionally drawn along the [[Ural Mountains]]; its western boundary varies, and narrow definitions include Belarus, Russia and Ukraine. Its cultural traditions have been shaped by the Slavs and by [[Eastern Christianity]]. During the Cold War the term denoted the communist states of the [[Eastern Bloc]], separated from the West by the Iron Curtain. From 1945 to 1989 most of the region was under communist rule, and many of its countries later joined NATO and the European Union. The term is sometimes considered pejorative, and Central and Eastern Europe is sometimes used as a more neutral grouping.

Theater of World War II in Europe, fought between the Axis powers and the [[Soviet Union]] from June 22, 1941, when Germany invaded in Operation Barbarossa, until the capture of Berlin in May 1945. Of the estimated 70–85 million deaths attributed to the war, around 30 million occurred on this front. The Battle of Stalingrad, the bloodiest battle of the war, was a key turning point, and the Battle of Kursk crippled German offensive capabilities. Historian Geoffrey Roberts noted that more than 80 percent of all combat in the Second World War took place on the Eastern Front. Nazi military operations included mass deportations, starvation and massacres. The United States and United Kingdom provided substantial material aid to the Soviet Union through Lend-Lease, though they sent no ground troops.
